Similar movements in loop C have been reported for multiple Cys-loop receptors
and linked to channel activation32,43. Loop C typically adopts an outward-facing
conformation in the closed state and moves inward to cap the canonical binding site
upon agonist binding, or in the case of SsCl, in response to pH changes
(Supplementary Fig. 26). In SsCl, the ECD also adopts an overall more compact
arrangement in the partially open, open, and desensitized states compared to the
closed state (Supplementary Movie 7).
Below loop C, an additional hydrophobic interaction is observed between M194
from loop C and M169 from loop F of the complementary subunit. This interaction
appears to stabilize the ECD at acidic pH, as it is present only in the structures at pH
6.5. At pH 9, these residues are positioned farther apart, suggesting that the pH-induced
conformational changes disrupt this interaction (Figure 5f, Supplementary Fig. 24).
Furthermore, Loop F exhibits pronounced movement in the partially open and open
states, but not in the desensitized state. Specifically, R171 within loop F moves inward,
towards the traditional orthosteric binding-pocket (Supplementary Movie 8). Loop F is a
critical component of the ligand-binding region, contributing to the complementary face
of the orthosteric site in Cys-loop receptors.
The structural observations and functional results outlined above provide initial
insight into the distinct pH-sensing and gating mechanisms of SsCl. Collectively, these
results highlight a cluster of histidine and glutamic acid residues within the binding-like
region of the ECD that influence pH sensing and are predicted to form an important
component involved in responding to pH changes. pH-induced activation is also
associated with conformational changes throughout the ECD, including loop C and loop
F, which are known to contribute to ligand binding and channel gating across pLGICs.
Moreover, the binding-like region is likely part of a broader pH-sensing network
distributed throughout the channel. To fully understand the complexity of pH sensing
and the mechanism of pH-dependent channel activation, additional studies exploring
other regions of the channel will be required.
In summary, SsCl is an atypical member of the pLGIC family. It is an anionic
chloride-channel activated by alkaline pH in a concentration-dependent manner. SsCl
only shares a low sequence conservation with its nearest relatives, such as insect
pHCls and the invertebrate GluCl. Despite this, it adopts an architectural fold that is
typical for the pLGIC family and shares some similar gating mechanisms, including a
pore constriction at the 9’ position in the closed state. An important feature of SsCl is the
predicted pH-sensing residues within the binding-like region, where non-conserved
histidine and glutamic acid residues contribute to pH-dependent channel activation. This
region is likely part of a broader pH-sensing network that requires further investigation.
IVM can also activate the channel by binding within the TM domains in a similar binding
mode to the one observed in GluCl, indicating a common mechanism of ligand
recognition. Structurally, IVM greatly widens the pore radius, thus facilitating the flow of
chloride ions through the channel. However, distinctive conformations are observed that
depend on the pH environment. At pH 6.5 in the presence of IVM, the pore constricts
around the selectivity filter, thus limiting ion flow. In contrast, at pH 9 with IVM, the pore
is wide open. A summarized view of the SsCl structural states is shown in Figure 7.
Another unusual feature in SsCl is the electrostatic surface potential. It is predominantly
electronegative in the ECD and upper part of TMD; however, it becomes neutral about
halfway down the pore and is positive near the selectivity filter. The helix dipole effect
likely contributes to lowering the energy barrier for ion permeation through the
constriction of the selectivity filter. Collectively, these findings highlight structural and
functional features of SsCl, and provide initial insights into the channel’s mechanisms,
which warrant further investigation. These findings could inform the development of
novel and more effective therapeutics targeting scabies.

filtration column (Cytiva) pre-equilibrated with a running buffer containing 10 mM bis-
trispropane at pH 9 or 6.5, 150 mM NaCl, and 0.15% n-undecyl-β-D-maltoside.
The
eluted fractions were analysed by SDS-PAGE and pooled. The resulting fraction was
concentrated on an Amicon concentrator with a molecular weight cut-off of 100 kDa.
This solution was then directly used to prepare EM grids. For the determination of the
IVM-bound structures, 10 g/mL IVM was added during all purification steps starting
from solubilization.
Cryo-EM sample preparation
Cryo-EM grids were prepared using QUANTIFOIL® R 1.2/1.3 holey carbon films
on 300 mesh copper supports. Before the sample application, grids were glow-
discharged for 60 s at 0.39 mBar and 15 mA, using a PELCO easiGlow™ Glow
Discharge System. Subsequently, 3 μL of purified protein sample ranging from 2 to 3
mg/mL was applied to each grid, which was then blotted for either 5.4 or 5.6 s at 4 °C
and 95% relative humidity using a Leica EM GP2 automatic plunge freezer. Grids were
immediately vitrified by plunge-freezing into liquid ethane and stored in liquid nitrogen.
Cryo-EM data acquisition
Cryo-EM datasets for the pH 9, pH 9 with IVM, and pH 6.5 with IVM conditions
were collected on a Titan Krios transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher
Scientific) operating at 300 kV with a Gatan BioQuantum energy filter (operated at 20
eV) and a Gatan K3 direct electron detector at the Electron Bio-Imaging Centre (eBIC),
Diamond Light Source, Harwell, UK. The dataset corresponding to the pH 6.5 (closed
state) condition was acquired on a JEOL CryoARM 300 transmission electron
microscope (JEOL Ltd.) operated at 300 kV with an Omega filter and K3 direct electron
detector, at the VIB-VUB Facility for Bio Electron Cryogenic Microscopy (BECM),
Brussels, Belgium. Specifications for data collection can be found in the Supplementary
Table 1.
Cryo-EM data processing
Datasets were processed according to the workflow outlined in Supplementary
Fig. 6. Initial processing was performed in RELION 5.0 (ref 58). Raw movies were
motion-corrected and dose-weighted using RELION’s implementation of MotionCor259,
and contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated with CTFFIND460.
Particle picking was conducted externally using crYOLO61, employing the general pre-
trained model with dataset-specific adjustments to picking threshold and particle size.
Picked coordinates were imported into RELION for particle extraction with initial
downsampling to accelerate processing. Extracted particles underwent multiple rounds
of 2D classification to remove poorly aligned classes and particles lacking clear
structural features of a pentameric channel. Selected particles were used to generate
an initial 3D model, followed by unsupervised 3D classification in C1. Particles from
well-resolved classes were then re-extracted at the original pixel size.
Further steps were carried out in cryoSPARC62. Another 2D classification step
was performed, followed by ab initio reconstruction, non-uniform63, and local refinement
in C1 symmetry. Symmetry analysis of the channel confirmed C5 symmetry, which was
applied in the final rounds of global and local refinement. Global and local CTF
refinement were performed to enhance overall map resolution and alignment fidelity.
Maps were visualized using UCSF ChimeraX64.
Model building, refinement, and validation
An initial reference model was generated using AlphaFold2 (or AlphaFold365) and
used as the starting point for model building. Construction began with a single subunit,
which was first rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM map using the ‘fit’ tool in UCSF
ChimeraX. Interactive model building was then carried out in COOT66 to resolve
discrepancies and improve the overall fit. Refinement proceeded iteratively within the
Doppio suite (CCP-EM67), beginning with TEMPy-REFF68 to optimize model-to-map
agreement. This was followed by successive refinement cycles using
Refmac/Servalcat69, interspersed with detailed interactive model building in COOT. Final
optimization of local conformations was achieved using ISOLDE70 through interactive
molecular dynamics flexible fitting. Once the single-subunit model met refinement and
validation criteria, C5 symmetry was applied to reconstruct the full assembly.
Comprehensive validation was performed using Doppio’s integrated pipeline to assess
stereochemistry, fit-to-density, and sequence fidelity. Additional validation of sequence
registration was carried out using FindMySequence and CheckMySequence, enabling
correction and confirmation of residue-level assignments within the density. Figures
were prepared using PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 3.0,
Schrödinger, LLC.) and UCSF ChimeraX.
Pore analysis with HOLE
Pore dimensions were analyzed using the HOLE program71. The SsCl refined
atomic models were used as inputs, and the pore axis was defined manually by
selecting points along the central channel for each structure. HOLE was run using
default parameters to calculate the pore profile, and the resulting radius plot was used
to identify constriction sites and estimate the pore diameter along the channel axis. Pore
radius profiles were plotted using GraphPad Prism, and structural figures were
generated with PyMOL.
Electrostatics calculations
Electrostatics calculations were performed using the Adaptive Poisson–
Boltzmann Solver (APBS)72 at the experimental pH values of 6.5 and 9. Protonation
states were assigned using PROPKA through the PDB2PQR pipeline with Amber force-
field parameters. The linearized Poisson–Boltzmann equation was solved under single
Debye–Hückel boundary conditions. The protein dielectric constant was set to 2.0, and
the solvent dielectric constant to 78.0. Atomic charges were mapped to the grid using
cubic B-spline discretization. Calculations were performed at 310 K in the presence of
two mobile ion species (Na⁺ and Cl⁻), each at 0.15 M, with ion radii of 2.0 Å for Na⁺ and
1.8 Å for Cl⁻. The membrane environment was not included in these calculations. The
APBS results were visualized as Surface potentials and Electrostatic isocontours.
Residue selection for pH-sensing and gating analysis
The burial percentage and pKₐ values of all titratable residues were calculated
using PROPKA49 (via PDB2PQR, with Amber force-field parameters). Cysteine pairs
forming disulfide bonds were excluded from the analysis. In addition, residues within the
transmembrane domain were not considered since this study focused on the
extracellular region, known as important for binding and channel modulation in other
pLGICs.
State-dependent changes were identified by detailed structural analysis and by
comparing the predicted pKₐ values and solvent exposure between the two pH
conditions. Residues exhibiting shifts in pKₐ together with changes in burial or solvent
accessibility were flagged as potential candidates, as such features indicate altered
interactions and/or structural rearrangements associated with pH-dependent
conformational transitions. Candidate residues were further investigated in the three-
dimensional structures to inspect local interactions, including hydrogen bonds,
electrostatic contacts, and clustering with neighbouring titratable groups. Known
functional roles of analogous regions in related pH-sensitive receptors were considered
to guide interpretation.
mRNA synthesis for electrophysiology
For expression in Xenopus oocytes, the full-length sequence of SsCl was
subcloned into pGEM-HE73 using EcoRI and HindIII restriction sites. SsCl was
engineered the same way as for the pFastBac expression construct. The plasmid was
linearized with PstI and transcribed with the mMESSAGE mMACHINE T7 ULTRA
Transcription kit. The typical yield of cRNA was around 1.5 g/L. Point mutants of SsCl

(Agilent). Mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing (LGC Genomics, Germany).

PARIS SARCLAY Institut des Neurosciences, bât. 151, 151 route de la Rotonde 91400

All recordings were conducted using the automated TEVC system, HiClamp

interpretation possible within the limitation. While some uncertainty could remain due to
resolution, the consistency across multiple map treatments supports confidence in the
overall assignment. To reflect this, we have clarified in the manuscript (lines 243-245) that
the pore radius for this state was carefully interpreted due to low resolution.
-While IVM can be confidently fit into the maps, details of the binding pocket at this
resolution appear over-interpreted. Based on the maps, only two side chains (e.g. K264 and
D277) can be defined unambiguously in the pocket. Figure 3, as presented, suggests
considerably more certainty than is warranted. I recommend the authors indicate explicitly
the limitations of the data, and consider showing only mainchain positions and general
pocket regions, omitting detailed side chains unless their orientation is clearly supported.
Response: The densities in the IVM pocket region were carefully examined before
confidently reporting the residues involved in IVM binding pocket. We believe some
confusion may arise from the Sup. Fig. 14 (now renumbered to 15), which shows only the
side chains of K264 and D277 as part of a focused discussion on these residues. To avoid
any misunderstanding and better represent the data, we have now included a new
supplementary figure (new Sup. Fig. 14, line 217) displaying the cryo-EM densities for all
residues within the IVM pocket for both structures at pH 6.5 and pH 9 with IVM. This aims to
clarify the discussed data that is supported by the density. In the new updated
supplementary material, the figures from old 14 on were renumbered accordingly.
2. Identification of M4
-Can the authors clarify how they are assigning the M4 segment in the pH 9 conditions? In
Supplemental Figure 10, there does not appear to be continuous density connecting M4 to
the rest of the structure. A clear explanation, and if possible, supporting visual evidence,
would be helpful.
Response: The identification of the M4 segment in the cryo-EM maps at pH 9 was based on
the highly conserved overall position of this segment among Cys-loop receptors. In
Supplementary Figure 10, we present the M4 segment in a side view alongside a bottom view
with a slice through the structure. Due to this slicing, the connections between the
transmembrane helices are not visible if the connecting loop is positioned at the bottom of
the structure. For clarity, we have included a dotted line in the side view indicating the plane
at which the bottom view is sliced.
3. Hourglass conformation
-The “hourglass” channel profile is described as unexpected by the authors, but similar
conformations have been observed in other pLGICs. The manuscript should clarify that this
structural arrangement, while potentially unprecedented among anionic pLGICs, is not
unique in the broader pLGIC family.
Response: The discussion of this unique conformation for an anionic channel and
comparison to cationic channels is included within the text, constituting its own paragraph
within the ‘ion-conducting pathway and selectivity’ section (lines 260-269).
As this is an interesting find we wish to draw the reader’s attention to, it is also
included within the abstract (lines 31-33) “The desensitized structure adopts an unexpected
“hourglass” conformation, suggesting the gating mechanisms may be more related to
cation-selective channels”.
We believe these references are su6icient to communicate to the reader that this
conformation is unexpected and indeed unique for anionic channels, however that the
conformation has been noted before for cationic channels such as the nicotinic
acetylcholine receptor.
4. Micrograph quality and data processing
- There are concerning artifacts visible in several representative micrographs (e.g., a vertical
black streak in the pH 6.5 closed, other artifacts in pH 6.5 IVM, and a white vertical line in pH
9). Were the images properly gain-corrected? Please clarify the source of these artifacts and
their implications.
Response: We thank the referee for highlighting these details. All micrographs were properly
gain-corrected prior to further processing using the gain reference file obtained before the
particular data collection. The vertical streaks and lines observed in some micrographs are
known artifacts that can arise from beam-induced motion, detector defects, or residual
issues in image acquisition. These artifacts are localized and do not a6ect the overall dataset
quality or the final reconstructions, as they are mitigated during the subsequent steps in the
data processing. We have reviewed the micrographs carefully and confirm that the a6ected
images constitute a small fraction of the dataset and do not bias the results. We have
updated the example micrographs in Sup.Fig. 6 changing to images that better represent the
datasets, and now we are showing motion corrected images.
- The workflow states three rounds of 2D classification, yet only four 2D classes remain. Why
so few? All 2D classes should be presented with selected classes clearly marked.
Response: Three rounds of 2D classification were performed in Relion with a large number
of initial classes (typically 50–100). We chose to present only the selected classes
representing the predominant particle views in our datasets. Displaying a subset of well-
defined classes is common practice in cryo-EM studies to focus on relevant particle
populations without redundancy. Additionally, several 2D classes discarded during the initial
classifications corresponded to dust or empty micelles, common contaminants that are
irrelevant for further processing, and were therefore excluded from the presentation in Sup.
Fig. 6. We have updated the Sup. Fig. 6 legend accordingly for clarity.
-The approach to 3D classification appears limited; what was the rationale for the number of
classes, and could more exhaustive searching improve map quality or state separation?
-The total particle numbers for each 3D class should be provided for transparency and
reproducibility.
Response: Initially, we tested di6erent numbers of 3D classes to explore dataset
heterogeneity, but higher number of classes did not improve the final reconstructions, likely
due to insu6icient number of particles in each class. Therefore, for some datasets, two
classes were adequate, while four classes were used for datasets with, for example, more
contamination such as empty micelles. This strategy balances computational e6iciency
with meaningful state separation. We acknowledge that cryo-EM processing is non-linear
and highly dependent on dataset characteristics, and thus flexible approaches are often
necessary. In addition, we have now included total particle numbers for each 3D class in
Sup. Fig. 6, for transparency.
-Scale bars should be added to all micrographs.
Response: Scale bars have been added to the micrographs present in Sup. Figure 6.
-3DFSC plots should be included for each map so that map anisotropy can be assessed.
Response: 3DFSC plots have been included for each map in Sup. Figure 6.
5. Electrophysiology data reporting
-For most electrophysiological experiments, “n ≥ 3” is listed as the number of replicates.
For clarity and full transparency, the explicit number of repeats for each condition should be
stated in all figure legends and results.
Response: For all electrophysiology data we have reported the minimum number of repeats
in the figure legends, as is common for publications using this technique. We have
additionally displayed the explicit number of repeats for each condition within the figures,
dependent on the type of data being depicted.
For all electrophysiology data, we have included a figure in the supplementary
material that includes a table displaying all numerical information for each condition,
including the explicit number of repeats (example: Sup. Figure 22).
Additionally, for all electrophysiology data represented as bar graphs we have
displayed the individual data points on the graphs. This provides greater transparency as it
visually presents the number of replicates, as well as the spread of the data (examples:
Figure 6 panels C and F).
As all figures with functional electrophysiology data contain multiple single and triple
mutants, listing all mutations and their exact number of replicates would be too extensive.
We believe the current display method to be su6icient, with all numerical information
provided clearly in supplementary figure 22.
